notes.front: What is SMS-based authentication in Microsoft Entra ID?
notes.back: Signing in with a verification code sent by text message (short message service) to the user’s registered mobile number.
notes.explanation: Unlike some phone options, it can serve as a primary method as well as a secondary one for MFA or password reset.
notes.example: Like a bank texting you a six-digit code that you type into its website before it shows your balance.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Phone”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is voice call verification in Microsoft Entra ID?
notes.back: An automated call to the user’s registered phone number, in which the user presses # on the keypad to complete sign-in.
notes.explanation: It is offered as a secondary form of verification during password reset or Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication.
notes.example: Like a building’s intercom that rings your desk phone and asks you to press a key to let a visitor in.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Phone”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is OATH, as used in Microsoft Entra ID?
notes.back: Open Authentication: an open standard that specifies how time-based one-time password codes are generated.
notes.explanation: Because it is an open standard, the codes can be produced either by software or by hardware.
notes.example: Like an agreed recipe that any baker can follow: different kitchens, same result.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “OATH”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a software OATH token?
notes.back: An app, such as Microsoft Authenticator, that generates OATH codes from a secret key (seed) that Microsoft Entra ID generates.
notes.explanation: The seed is entered into the app and used to generate each code.
notes.example: Like a phone app that shows a fresh number every half-minute for logging in to a game account.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “OATH”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is an OATH TOTP hardware token?
notes.back: A small key-fob device that displays a code which refreshes at a fixed interval, giving a second factor for authentication.
notes.explanation: It generates the same kind of time-based codes as a software token, but in a dedicated device.
notes.example: Like the little keyring gadget some banks once posted to customers, with a screen showing a number.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “OATH”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a Temporary Access Pass (TAP)?
notes.back: A time-limited passcode issued by an administrator, used to sign in and register other authentication methods.
notes.explanation: It gives a user a way in when they have no other method yet, or have lost the ones they had.
notes.example: Like a day pass from reception that lets you in long enough to collect your permanent badge.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Other authentication methods”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is QR code authentication in Microsoft Entra ID?
notes.back: Signing in by scanning a unique QR code, which can be printed on a badge, and entering a numeric personal identification number.
notes.explanation: It spares users from typing complex usernames and passwords.
notes.example: Like tapping a loyalty card at a till and keying in a short number instead of filling in a form.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Other authentication methods”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is an email one-time passcode (OTP) in Microsoft Entra ID?
notes.back: A verification code sent to the user’s email address.
notes.explanation: It is used as a secondary method during self-service password reset and can also be set up for guest sign-in.
notes.example: Like the code an online shop emails you to confirm it is really you changing the delivery address.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Other authentication methods”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Platform Credential for macOS?
notes.back: A phishing-resistant credential on Mac devices, unlocked with Touch ID or a password, giving passwordless sign-in and single sign-on across apps.
notes.explanation: The credential is backed by the device’s Secure Enclave.
notes.example: Like a Mac that signs you in to your work apps once you touch the fingerprint key, with no password to type.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Other authentication methods”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Authenticator Lite?
notes.back: A capability built into familiar apps such as Outlook mobile that lets users complete MFA without the separate Authenticator app.
notes.explanation: Users approve push notifications or use time-based codes inside an app they already have.
notes.example: Like a mail app on your phone that pops up “Was this you?” when you sign in on a laptop.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Other authentication methods”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are external authentication methods in Microsoft Entra ID?
notes.back: A way to connect a non-Microsoft multifactor authentication provider to Microsoft Entra ID so users can satisfy MFA with it.
notes.explanation: The organisation can keep using an authentication solution it already has in place.
notes.example: Like a hotel accepting your airline’s frequent-flyer card as proof of identity instead of issuing its own.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Other authentication methods”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a device-bound passkey?
notes.back: A passkey whose private key is created and stored on a single physical device and never leaves it.
notes.explanation: Microsoft Authenticator and FIDO2 security keys are Microsoft’s examples.
notes.example: Like a house key that has no copies: whoever has the single key can get in.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Passkeys (FIDO2) authentication method in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Types of passkeys” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: The private key is created and stored on a single physical device and never leaves it. Examples: - Microsoft Authenticator - FIDO2 Security keys

notes.front: What is a synced passkey?
notes.back: A passkey whose encrypted private key is synced to a cloud passkey provider, so the user’s other devices can use it.
notes.explanation: The key is encrypted on the local device before it is synced and stored with the provider.
notes.example: Like a digital car key that appears on both your phone and your watch because they share one account.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Passkeys (FIDO2) authentication method in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Types of passkeys” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: This encrypted key is then synced and stored in the cloud passkey provider. Other devices authenticated with the passkey provider may then use the passkey. This may differ depending on the provider.

notes.front: What is push notification with number matching in Microsoft Authenticator?
notes.back: The app sends a push notification, and the user must type the number shown on the sign-in screen into the app to approve.
notes.explanation: It is used when Authenticator acts as a secondary factor for MFA or password reset.
notes.example: Like a parcel locker that only opens when you type the code shown on the courier’s screen, not just press “Accept”.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Microsoft Authenticator”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is certificate-based authentication (CBA) in Microsoft Entra ID?
notes.back: Authenticating directly with X.509 certificates against the user’s Microsoft Entra identity.
notes.explanation: It gives a cloud-native approach that does not need federated infrastructure.
notes.example: Like a smart card with an embedded certificate that a reader checks against the issuer’s records.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Certificate-based authentication”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID?
notes.back: Preconfigured security settings from Microsoft that help protect an organisation from common identity attacks such as password spray, replay and phishing.
notes.explanation: Microsoft offers them to everyone because it knows managing security can be difficult.
notes.example: Like a new flat that comes with a door lock and smoke alarm already fitted, before you add anything of your own.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: Security defaults make it easier to help protect your organization from identity-related attacks like password spray, replay, and phishing common in today's environments. Microsoft is making these preconfigured security settings available to everyone, because we know managing security can be difficult.

notes.front: What is self-service password reset (SSPR)?
notes.back: A Microsoft Entra feature that lets users change or reset their own password, with no administrator or help desk involvement.
notes.explanation: Users who are locked out or have forgotten a password can unblock themselves, which reduces help desk calls and lost productivity.
notes.example: Like a hotel kiosk that reissues your lost room key after you answer its checks, without queueing at reception.
notes.source: Microsoft, “How it works: Microsoft Entra self-service password reset”, “How it works: Microsoft Entra self-service password reset” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: gives users the ability to change or reset their password, with no administrator or help desk involvement. If a user's account is locked or they forget their password, they can follow prompts to unblock themselves and get back to work. This ability reduces help desk calls and loss of productivity

notes.front: What is password writeback?
notes.back: Writing password changes made in Microsoft Entra ID back to an on-premises directory, configured through Microsoft Entra Connect cloud sync.
notes.explanation: It applies in hybrid environments, where users also exist in an on-premises directory.
notes.example: Like updating your address on a council website and having it copied automatically into the old paper register at the town hall.
notes.source: Microsoft, “How it works: Microsoft Entra self-service password reset”, “On-premises integration” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: In a hybrid environment, you can configure Microsoft Entra Connect cloud sync to write password change events back from Microsoft Entra ID to an on-premises directory.

notes.front: What is Microsoft Entra Password Protection?
notes.back: A feature that detects and blocks known weak passwords and their variants, and can also block weak terms specific to your organisation.
notes.explanation: Weak or insecure passwords are often still used even when users are given guidance.
notes.example: Like a website that refuses “Summer2026!” when you try to set it as your new password.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Eliminate bad passwords using Microsoft Entra Password Protection”, “Eliminate bad passwords using Microsoft Entra Password Protection” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: but weak or insecure passwords are often still used. Microsoft Entra Password Protection detects and blocks known weak passwords and their variants, and can also block other weak terms that are specific to your organization.

notes.front: What is the global banned password list?
notes.back: Microsoft’s list of commonly used weak or compromised base terms, found through Microsoft Entra security telemetry.
notes.explanation: The Microsoft Entra ID Protection team keeps analysing telemetry and adds weak terms as it finds them.
notes.example: Like a national list of words no one may use as a car’s personalised number plate.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Eliminate bad passwords using Microsoft Entra Password Protection”, “Global banned password list” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: The Microsoft Entra ID Protection team constantly analyzes Microsoft Entra security telemetry data looking for commonly used weak or compromised passwords. Specifically, the analysis looks for base terms that often are used as the basis for weak passwords. When weak terms are found, they're added to the *global banned password list*.

notes.front: What is the custom banned password list?
notes.back: A list of an organisation’s own terms, such as brand or product names, blocked on top of the global list.
notes.explanation: Some organisations want to add their own customisations to improve security beyond the global list.
notes.example: Like a school adding its own name and mascot to the list of passwords pupils may not choose.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Eliminate bad passwords using Microsoft Entra Password Protection”, “Custom banned password list” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: Some organizations want to improve security and add their own customizations on top of the global banned password list. To add your own entries, you can use the *custom banned password list*.

notes.front: What is a password spray attack?
notes.back: An attack that tries only a few of the weakest known passwords against each of many accounts.
notes.explanation: Trying few passwords per account lets the attacker search quickly for an easy account while avoiding detection thresholds.
notes.example: Like a burglar who tries the single most common key on every door in a street, rather than picking one lock for hours.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Eliminate bad passwords using Microsoft Entra Password Protection”, “Password spray attacks and third-party compromised password lists” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: Instead, most password spray attacks submit only a few of the known weakest passwords against each of the accounts in an enterprise. This technique allows the attacker to quickly search for an easily compromised account and avoid potential detection thresholds.

notes.front: Why are passwords problematic when used as the only form of authentication?
notes.back: Passwords easy enough to remember are easy to compromise; strong ones are hard to remember and cost productivity when forgotten.
notes.explanation: The course says passwords should be supplemented or replaced by more secure Microsoft Entra methods.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Passwords”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication, which factor category does a password belong to?
notes.back: Something you know.
notes.explanation: Microsoft Entra MFA requires two or more of the listed kinds of method.
notes.source: Microsoft, “How it works: Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication”, “How it works: Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication works by requiring two or more of the following authentication methods: * Something you know, typically a password.

notes.front: In Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication, which factor category does a phone or hardware key belong to?
notes.back: Something you have: a trusted device that’s not easily duplicated.
notes.explanation: A phone or a hardware key are the examples given.
notes.source: Microsoft, “How it works: Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication”, “How it works: Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: Something you have, such as a trusted device that's not easily duplicated, like a phone or hardware key.

notes.front: In Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication, which factor category does a fingerprint or face scan belong to?
notes.back: Something you are (biometrics).
notes.explanation: Biometrics like a fingerprint or face scan are this third category.
notes.source: Microsoft, “How it works: Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication”, “How it works: Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: Something you are - biometrics like a fingerprint or face scan.

notes.front: Microsoft’s multifactor authentication overview on GitHub lists one more MFA verification method than the Microsoft Learn training unit. Which one?
notes.back: QR code.
notes.explanation: The training unit’s list stops at twelve methods and omits QR code; lists like this change, so check the current page.
notes.source: Microsoft, “How it works: Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication”, “Available verification methods” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: * Passkey in Microsoft Authenticator * QR code * Certificate-based authentication (when configured for multifactor authentication)

notes.front: What does Microsoft recommend users move to instead of text messages or voice calls for MFA?
notes.back: More modern methods such as Microsoft Authenticator or passkeys.
notes.explanation: The course states the recommendation directly: move away from text and voice for MFA.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Phone”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Can voice call verification be used as a primary form of authentication in Microsoft Entra ID?
notes.back: No; only as a secondary form, during password reset or MFA.
notes.explanation: SMS, by contrast, can be primary as well as secondary.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Phone”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An OATH TOTP hardware token displays a code that refreshes every {{c1::30 or 60}} seconds.
notes.explanation: A new code at each interval is what makes the code time-based.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “OATH”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Are software and hardware OATH tokens primary or secondary methods in Microsoft Entra ID?
notes.back: Secondary: they verify an identity during password reset or Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication.
notes.explanation: Neither kind of OATH token can be used as the primary sign-in method.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “OATH”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two situations where a Temporary Access Pass is useful?
notes.back: Onboarding new users; helping users recover access after losing their credentials.
notes.explanation: Both are cases where the user has no working method to sign in and register a new one.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Other authentication methods”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: For which users is QR code authentication primarily designed?
notes.back: Frontline workers on shared devices.
notes.explanation: Scanning a badge and entering a short numeric code replaces typing complex usernames and passwords.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Other authentication methods”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides self-service password reset, what else can email one-time passcodes be configured for?
notes.back: Guest user sign-in.
notes.explanation: Email OTP is otherwise a secondary method used only during password reset.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Other authentication methods”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What example does the course give of a non-Microsoft MFA provider that external authentication methods can connect?
notes.back: Duo Security, for example (the course names one other product too).
notes.explanation: External authentication methods let users satisfy MFA with a solution the organisation already has.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Other authentication methods”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a passkey (FIDO2), which key is registered with Microsoft Entra ID, and which is kept by the user?
notes.back: The public key is registered with Entra ID; the private key is stored securely by the user’s authenticator.
notes.explanation: Passkeys use public key cryptography, with a key pair created during registration.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Passkeys (FIDO2)”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why are passkeys phishing-resistant?
notes.back: They are bound to the specific site where they were registered, so they can’t be used on a look-alike site.
notes.explanation: Even a convincing fake sign-in page cannot use a passkey created for the real one.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Passkeys (FIDO2)”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two examples of synced passkey providers?
notes.back: Apple iCloud Keychain and Google Password Manager.
notes.explanation: These are the cloud passkey providers Microsoft gives as examples.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Passkeys (FIDO2) authentication method in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Types of passkeys” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: Synced passkeys do not support attestation. Examples: - Apple iCloud Keychain - Google Password Manager

notes.front: Which type of passkey does not support attestation?
notes.back: Synced passkeys.
notes.explanation: If attestation is enabled in Microsoft Entra ID, only device-bound passkeys are allowed and synced passkeys are excluded.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Passkeys (FIDO2) authentication method in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Types of passkeys” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: If attestation is enabled, only device-bound passkeys are allowed; synced passkeys are excluded.

notes.front: Which Microsoft Authenticator mode gives phishing-resistant sign-in using the user’s biometric or device personal identification number?
notes.back: Passkey sign-in, using a device-bound passkey registered in the app.
notes.explanation: A passkey held in Authenticator stays on that one device.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Microsoft Authenticator”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In which Microsoft Authenticator mode does the user match a number from the sign-in screen and confirm with a biometric instead of typing a password?
notes.back: Passwordless sign-in.
notes.explanation: No password is entered at any point in this mode.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Microsoft Authenticator”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Microsoft Authenticator mode, used as a secondary factor for MFA or password reset, sends a prompt that the user approves in the app?
notes.back: Push notification with number matching.
notes.explanation: The user types the number shown on screen into the app to approve.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Microsoft Authenticator”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides passkeys, passwordless sign-in and push notifications, what else can the Microsoft Authenticator app generate?
notes.back: OATH verification codes.
notes.explanation: This makes the app a software OATH token as well.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Microsoft Authenticator”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which kind of attack does number matching in Microsoft Authenticator help prevent?
notes.back: MFA fatigue attacks.
notes.explanation: The user has to enter the number shown on the sign-in screen, rather than simply approve a prompt.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Require all users to register for Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: When users sign in and are prompted to perform multifactor authentication, they see a screen providing them with a number to enter in the Microsoft Authenticator app. This measure helps prevent users from falling for MFA fatigue attacks.

notes.front: What kind of infrastructure does Microsoft Entra certificate-based authentication remove the need for?
notes.back: Federated infrastructure, such as Active Directory Federation Services.
notes.explanation: Certificates are checked directly against the Entra identity, a simplified cloud-native approach.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Certificate-based authentication”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How can certificate-based authentication be used in Microsoft Entra ID?
notes.back: As a primary passwordless method and, when configured, as a multifactor authentication method.
notes.explanation: It appears on both the primary and the MFA side of the method table.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Certificate-based authentication”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why are traditional MFA methods such as SMS or email one-time passwords increasingly vulnerable?
notes.back: To remote phishing, where attackers use social engineering and AI-driven tools to steal credentials without touching the user’s device.
notes.explanation: The course links this to the rise of AI-driven cyberattacks.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Phishing-resistant authentication”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How do phishing-resistant methods stop a credential being used on a fraudulent look-alike site?
notes.back: The credential is bound to the website origin (domain) where it was registered, and the authenticator checks the requesting site’s domain.
notes.explanation: They rely on public key cryptography, so the credential also can’t be replayed or shared with attackers.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Phishing-resistant authentication”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which phishing-resistant method in Microsoft Entra ID is for macOS devices?
notes.back: Platform Credential for macOS.
notes.explanation: It appears in Microsoft’s list of phishing-resistant methods alongside Windows Hello for Business.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Phishing-resistant authentication”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Are synced passkeys on Microsoft’s list of phishing-resistant methods?
notes.back: Yes, synced passkeys (FIDO2) are on the list, as are FIDO2 security keys and passkeys in Microsoft Authenticator.
notes.explanation: The list also includes Windows Hello for Business, Platform Credential for macOS and certificate-based authentication.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Phishing-resistant authentication”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which certificate-based method appears on Microsoft’s list of phishing-resistant methods?
notes.back: Certificate-based authentication (CBA).
notes.explanation: The list also includes Windows Hello for Business, Platform Credential for macOS and several kinds of passkey.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Phishing-resistant authentication”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why does Microsoft recommend phishing-resistant methods such as Windows Hello for Business, passkeys or CBA?
notes.back: Because they provide the most secure sign-in experience.
notes.explanation: Microsoft names Windows Hello for Business, passkeys, FIDO2 security keys and CBA as its examples.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Microsoft Entra authentication overview”, “Phishing-resistant authentication methods” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: Microsoft recommends using phishing-resistant authentication methods such as Windows Hello for Business, passkeys (FIDO2) and FIDO2 security keys, or certificate-based authentication (CBA) because they provide the most secure sign-in experience.

notes.front: What is the difference between a primary and a secondary authentication method in Microsoft Entra ID?
notes.back: A primary method can be the first factor at sign-in; a secondary method is only available during MFA or SSPR.
notes.explanation: The course’s table shows, for each method, whether it can be used in each role.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Primary and secondary authentication”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In which role can an email one-time passcode be used for Microsoft Entra users?
notes.back: Only as a secondary method for self-service password reset.
notes.explanation: It is neither a primary method nor an MFA method in the course’s table.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Primary and secondary authentication”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Can a Temporary Access Pass be used as a primary sign-in method?
notes.back: Yes; it can be primary, and it can also satisfy MFA.
notes.explanation: That is what lets a user with no other method sign in with it.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Primary and secondary authentication”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to Microsoft, what share of common identity-related attacks are stopped by using MFA and blocking legacy authentication?
notes.back: More than 99.9%.
notes.explanation: Microsoft’s stated goal is that every organisation has at least a basic level of security at no extra cost.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: Based on our learnings more than 99.9% of those common identity-related attacks are stopped by using multifactor authentication and blocking legacy authentication. Our goal is to ensure that all organizations have at least a basic level of security enabled at no extra cost.

notes.front: Under security defaults, which users must register for multifactor authentication?
notes.back: All users.
notes.explanation: Registration by everyone is the first of the basic controls security defaults include.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: These basic controls include: - Requiring all users to register for multifactor authentication

notes.front: Under security defaults, how often must the listed administrator roles do multifactor authentication?
notes.back: Every time they sign in, once registration is finished.
notes.explanation: Microsoft lists the specific administrator roles this applies to.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: After registration is finished, the following administrator roles will be required to do multifactor authentication every time they sign in:

notes.front: Under security defaults, who decides when an ordinary user is prompted for multifactor authentication?
notes.back: Microsoft, based on factors such as location, device, role and task.
notes.explanation: After registering, users are prompted for another authentication whenever necessary.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: After users complete registration, they'll be prompted for another authentication whenever necessary. Microsoft decides when a user is prompted for multifactor authentication, based on factors such as location, device, role, and task.

notes.front: Why do security defaults block legacy authentication protocols?
notes.back: Legacy authentication doesn’t support MFA, so an attacker could use an older protocol to bypass MFA.
notes.explanation: Microsoft says most compromising sign-in attempts come from legacy authentication.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: Today, most compromising sign-in attempts come from legacy authentication. Legacy authentication doesn't support multifactor authentication. Even if you have a multifactor authentication policy enabled on your directory, an attacker can authenticate by using an older protocol and bypass multifactor authentication.

notes.front: Which sign-in flow for devices with limited input, such as no keyboard, do security defaults block?
notes.back: Device code flow.
notes.explanation: Attackers can abuse it in phishing attacks by tricking users into entering a code on another device.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: Attackers can abuse device code flow in phishing attacks by tricking users into entering a code on another device. After security defaults are enabled in your tenant, authentication requests that use device code flow are blocked.

notes.front: Under security defaults, who must complete MFA to use the Azure portal, Microsoft Entra admin center, Azure PowerShell or Azure CLI?
notes.back: Any user accessing them, whether administrator or not.
notes.explanation: The policy covers Azure Resource Manager services, not only administrator accounts.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: This policy applies to all users who are accessing Azure Resource Manager services, whether they're an administrator or a user.

notes.front: Which two kinds of organisation are security defaults aimed at?
notes.back: Those wanting better security posture but unsure where to start, and those on the free tier of Microsoft Entra ID.
notes.explanation: Organisations with complex requirements are pointed to Conditional Access instead.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: Organizations who want to increase their security posture, but don't know how or where to start. - Organizations using the free tier of Microsoft Entra ID licensing.

notes.front: Are security defaults switched on in newly created tenants?
notes.back: Yes; they are enabled on all new tenants by default, with a 24-hour grace period before protections are enforced.
notes.explanation: The grace period lets customers access and provision the tenant before MFA is required.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: While security defaults is enabled on all new tenants by default, there is a 24‑hour grace period before protections are enforced. This allows customers to access and provision their tenant before MFA is required.

notes.front: Which licence must a user be assigned before they can use SSPR?
notes.back: A Microsoft Entra ID licence.
notes.explanation: SSPR capabilities also vary by licence tier.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe self-service password reset”, “How self-service password reset works”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides being licensed, who must enable a user for SSPR?
notes.back: An administrator.
notes.explanation: A user who isn’t enabled is told to contact their administrator to reset the password.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe self-service password reset”, “How self-service password reset works”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What must a user register before SSPR works for them?
notes.back: The authentication methods they want to use; two or more are recommended.
notes.explanation: More than one method keeps the user covered if one is unavailable.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe self-service password reset”, “How self-service password reset works”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When a user is enabled for SSPR, they must register at least {{c1::one}} authentication method.
notes.explanation: Microsoft highly recommends two or more, for flexibility if one is unavailable.
notes.source: Microsoft, “How it works: Microsoft Entra self-service password reset”, “Authentication methods” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: When a user is enabled for SSPR, they must register at least one authentication method. We highly recommend that you choose two or more authentication methods so that your users have more flexibility in case they're unable to access one method when they need it.

notes.front: What are the two phone-based methods available for SSPR?
notes.back: SMS and voice call.
notes.explanation: Microsoft Authenticator push notifications, OATH tokens and email OTP are also available.
notes.source: Microsoft, “How it works: Microsoft Entra self-service password reset”, “Authentication methods” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: * Microsoft Authenticator push notifications * Hardware OATH tokens (preview) * Software OATH tokens * Short Message Service (SMS) sign-in * Voice call * Email OTP

notes.front: How many authentication methods can an administrator require for SSPR?
notes.back: Either one or two.
notes.explanation: The same setting covers unlocking as well as resetting a password.
notes.source: Microsoft, “How it works: Microsoft Entra self-service password reset”, “Number of authentication methods required” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: You can configure the number of the available authentication methods a user must provide to reset or unlock their password. This value can be set to either *one* or *two*.

notes.front: Which SSPR method will be retired in March 2027?
notes.back: Security questions.
notes.explanation: After that date users can no longer reset passwords with them, so organisations should set up other methods first.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe self-service password reset”, “Authentication methods for SSPR”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What range of days can an administrator set for asking users to reconfirm their SSPR authentication information, and what does 0 mean?
notes.back: 0 to 730 days; 0 means users are never asked.
notes.explanation: The option is available only when users are required to register when signing in.
notes.source: Microsoft, “How it works: Microsoft Entra self-service password reset”, “Reconfirm authentication information” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: This option is only available if you enable the **Require users to register when signing in** option. Valid values to prompt a user to confirm their authentication information are from *0* to *730* days. Setting this value to *0* means that users are never asked to confirm their authentication information.

notes.front: With password writeback enabled, which kinds of hybrid users can reset their passwords?
notes.back: Federated, pass-through authentication, or password hash synchronised users.
notes.explanation: With writeback set to No, these same users can’t reset their passwords.
notes.source: Microsoft, “How it works: Microsoft Entra self-service password reset”, “Write back passwords to your on-premises directory” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: If the option is set to **Yes**, then writeback is enabled. Federated, pass-through authentication, or password hash synchronized users are able to reset their passwords. * If the option is set to **No**, then writeback is disabled. Federated, pass-through authentication, or password hash synchronized users aren't able to reset their passwords.

notes.front: Should organisations rely only on strong passwords enforced by Microsoft Entra Password Protection?
notes.back: No; they should also use other features such as Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication.
notes.explanation: Microsoft points to using multiple layers of security for sign-in events.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Eliminate bad passwords using Microsoft Entra Password Protection”, “Eliminate bad passwords using Microsoft Entra Password Protection” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: You should use other features like Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication, not just rely on strong passwords enforced by Microsoft Entra Password Protection. For more information on using multiple layers of security for your sign-in events

notes.front: Does an administrator need to enable the global banned password list?
notes.back: No. It applies automatically to all users in a tenant, needs no configuration and can’t be disabled.
notes.explanation: It is used whenever users change or reset their own password through Microsoft Entra ID.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Eliminate bad passwords using Microsoft Entra Password Protection”, “Global banned password list” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: The global banned password list is automatically applied to all users in a Microsoft Entra tenant. There's nothing to enable or configure, and can't be disabled. This global banned password list is applied to users when they change or reset their own password through Microsoft Entra ID.

notes.front: Is the global banned password list built from external data sources such as breach lists?
notes.back: No; it is based on Microsoft Entra security telemetry and analysis.
notes.explanation: It reflects analysis of Microsoft Entra security telemetry rather than outside lists.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Eliminate bad passwords using Microsoft Entra Password Protection”, “Global banned password list” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: The contents of the global banned password list aren't based on any external data source, but on the results of Microsoft Entra security telemetry and analysis.

notes.front: What are two kinds of term an organisation might put in its custom banned password list?
notes.back: Any two of: brand names; product names; locations such as headquarters; internal terms; company abbreviations.
notes.explanation: Microsoft says entries should focus on organisation-specific terms.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Eliminate bad passwords using Microsoft Entra Password Protection”, “Custom banned password list” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: Terms added to the custom banned password list should be focused on organizational-specific terms such as the following examples: - Brand names - Product names - Locations, such as company headquarters - Company-specific internal terms - Abbreviations that have specific company meaning

notes.front: How are the custom and global banned password lists used together?
notes.back: They are combined, and password changes or resets are validated against the combined set.
notes.explanation: Custom terms add to the global list rather than replacing it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Eliminate bad passwords using Microsoft Entra Password Protection”, “Custom banned password list” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: When terms are added to the custom banned password list, they're combined with the terms in the global banned password list. Password change or reset events are then validated against the combined set of these banned password lists.

notes.front: The custom banned password list is limited to a maximum of {{c1::1,000}} terms.
notes.explanation: It isn’t designed for blocking extremely large lists of passwords.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Eliminate bad passwords using Microsoft Entra Password Protection”, “Custom banned password list” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: The custom banned password list is limited to a maximum of 1,000 terms. It isn't designed for blocking extremely large lists of passwords.

notes.front: Is a password that contains a banned term always rejected?
notes.back: No; it may still be accepted if the overall password is strong enough.
notes.explanation: A scoring step decides the outcome, not the mere presence of a banned term.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Eliminate bad passwords using Microsoft Entra Password Protection”, “How are passwords evaluated” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: Even if a user's password contains a banned password, the password may be accepted if the overall password is otherwise strong enough.

notes.front: What two things happen when a new password is normalised?
notes.back: Uppercase letters become lowercase, then common character substitutions are made (such as 0 to o, $ to s).
notes.explanation: Normalising maps a small set of banned passwords to a much larger set of potentially weak ones.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Eliminate bad passwords using Microsoft Entra Password Protection”, “Step 1: Normalization” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: This technique allows for a small set of banned passwords to be mapped to a much larger set of potentially weak passwords. Normalization has the following two parts: * All uppercase letters are changed to lower case. * Then, common character substitutions are performed

notes.front: Fuzzy matching compares the normalised password with the banned lists using an edit distance of {{c1::one}}.
notes.explanation: A single changed, added or removed character therefore still counts as a match with a banned term.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Eliminate bad passwords using Microsoft Entra Password Protection”, “Fuzzy matching behavior” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: Fuzzy matching is used on the normalized password to identify if it contains a password found on either the global or the custom banned password lists. The matching process is based on an edit distance of one (1) comparison.

notes.front: Substring matching checks the normalised password for which terms?
notes.back: The user’s first and last name, and the tenant name.
notes.explanation: Tenant name matching isn’t done when passwords are validated on an on-premises domain controller.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Eliminate bad passwords using Microsoft Entra Password Protection”, “Substring matching (on specific terms)” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: Substring matching is used on the normalized password to check for the user's first and last name, and the tenant name. Tenant name matching isn't done when validating passwords on an AD DS domain controller for on-premises hybrid scenarios.

notes.front: How is a new password scored, and what score is needed?
notes.back: One point per banned term found, one point per remaining character; at least five points to be accepted.
notes.explanation: More remaining characters can lift a password containing banned terms over the threshold.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Eliminate bad passwords using Microsoft Entra Password Protection”, “Score Calculation” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: Each banned password found in a user's password is given one point. 1. Each remaining character that isn't part of a banned password is given one point. 1. A password must be at least five (5) points to be accepted.

notes.front: Why do most password spray attacks try each account only a few times?
notes.back: Trying one account many times would increase the chance of detection, through account lockout or other means.
notes.explanation: Account lockout is one of the ways repeated attempts on one account get noticed.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Eliminate bad passwords using Microsoft Entra Password Protection”, “Password spray attacks and third-party compromised password lists” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: Most password spray attacks don't attempt to attack any given individual account more than a few times. This behavior would increase the likelihood of detection, either via account lockout or other means.

notes.front: How does Microsoft Entra Password Protection defend against password spray attacks?
notes.back: It blocks all known weak passwords likely to be used in such attacks.
notes.explanation: Its global banned list is built from real-world security telemetry in Microsoft Entra ID.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Eliminate bad passwords using Microsoft Entra Password Protection”, “Password spray attacks and third-party compromised password lists” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: Microsoft Entra Password Protection efficiently blocks all known weak passwords likely to be used in password spray attacks. This protection is based on real-world security telemetry data from Microsoft Entra ID to build the global banned password list.

notes.front: Which on-premises Password Protection component forwards password policy download requests from domain controllers to Microsoft Entra ID?
notes.back: The proxy service, running on a domain-joined machine.
notes.explanation: Domain controllers never talk to the internet directly; all communication goes through the proxy service.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe password protection and management capabilities”, “On-premises integration”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which on-premises Password Protection component runs on domain controllers and validates password changes?
notes.back: The domain controller agent.
notes.explanation: It processes validation requests using the current policy downloaded from Microsoft Entra ID.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe password protection and management capabilities”, “On-premises integration”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A new employee starts on Monday with no phone app or security key registered yet. The admin wants her to sign in once and set up a passkey. What should the admin issue?
notes.back: D: a Temporary Access Pass.
notes.choices:
A) A voice call verification
B) An email one-time passcode
C) An OATH software token
D) A Temporary Access Pass
notes.choicesExplained: A cannot be a primary method. B is used for password reset, not first sign-in. C would itself need an app to be registered first.
notes.explanation: A time-limited pass lets a user sign in and register other methods, including passwordless ones, which suits onboarding.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Other authentication methods”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Warehouse staff share tablets at each shift change and struggle to type long usernames. Which method is designed for them?

A) External authentication methods
B) Certificate-based authentication
C) QR code authentication

notes.front: A company already uses a non-Microsoft MFA product for all staff and wants Microsoft Entra ID to accept it. What should it use?

A) Authenticator Lite
B) A Temporary Access Pass
C) External authentication methods
D) Security defaults

notes.explanation: They integrate a non-Microsoft MFA provider so users satisfy MFA with a solution already in place.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Other authentication methods”

notes.front: Factory workers may not carry smartphones on the floor, but need a second factor for MFA. Which device-based option fits?

A) A software OATH token
B) SMS-based authentication
C) An OATH TOTP hardware token

notes.front: A defence contractor enforces attestation on passkeys so it can check authenticator models. Which passkeys can its users register?

A) Both device-bound and synced passkeys
B) Synced passkeys only

notes.evidence: If attestation is enabled, only device-bound passkeys are allowed; synced passkeys are excluded.

notes.front: A user wants a passkey that is still available on her new phone after she replaces the old one, through her cloud account. Which type is this?
notes.back: C: a synced passkey.
notes.choices:
A) A device-bound passkey in Microsoft Authenticator
B) A FIDO2 security key
C) A synced passkey
D) An OATH hardware token

notes.evidence: This encrypted key is then synced and stored in the cloud passkey provider. Other devices authenticated with the passkey provider may then use the passkey.

notes.front: An attacker has a user’s password and keeps triggering sign-in prompts, hoping she will tap “Approve” out of annoyance. Which Authenticator behaviour makes this harder?
notes.back: D: number matching, where she must type the number shown on the sign-in screen.

A) OATH verification codes
B) Passkey sign-in on another device
C) SMS fallback
D) Number matching, where she must type the number shown on the sign-in screen
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C are other methods; none of them is the push-approval step the attacker is abusing.
notes.explanation: She cannot approve without seeing the attacker’s sign-in screen, so a stray tap does not work.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Microsoft Authenticator”

notes.front: A hospital wants only phishing-resistant sign-in for its clinicians. Which of these methods qualifies?

A) A FIDO2 security key

notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Phishing-resistant authentication”

notes.front: A bank wants a phishing-resistant, passwordless sign-in built into its staff’s Windows laptops. Which method fits?

A) Windows Hello for Business

notes.front: An admin wants a method staff can use as the first factor to sign in, without a password. Which of these cannot be used that way?

A) SMS sign-in

notes.front: A ten-person charity on the free tier of Microsoft Entra ID wants basic MFA protection without buying anything. What should it turn on?

A) Conditional Access policies
B) Security defaults
C) Temporary Access Passes for all staff
D) A custom banned password list

notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: Organizations who want to increase their security posture, but don't know how or where to start. - Organizations using the free tier of Microsoft Entra ID licensing.

notes.front: A firm wants MFA only when staff sign in from outside the corporate network or from personal devices. Which feature provides this?

B) Conditional Access policies

notes.front: A school syncs users from on-premises Active Directory using password hash synchronisation. Teachers who reset passwords in the cloud still can’t sign in to classroom PCs with the new one. What is missing?
notes.back: A: password writeback.
notes.choices:
A) Password writeback
B) Microsoft Entra Password Protection
C) A Temporary Access Pass
D) Number matching
notes.choicesExplained: B blocks weak passwords but does not copy changes on-premises. C is for sign-in and registration. D protects push approvals.

notes.front: Northwind, based in Leeds, sells a product called Beacon. What should its admin add to the custom banned password list?
notes.back: B: the base terms Northwind, Leeds and Beacon.
notes.choices:
A) Every variation, such as Northwind!1 and Beacon2026
B) The base terms Northwind, Leeds and Beacon
C) The 10,000 most common passwords on the internet
D) Nothing; custom terms replace the global list
notes.choicesExplained: A is wasteful and less secure. C exceeds the 1,000-term limit, and the list isn’t for large password lists. D is wrong: custom terms are combined with the global list.
notes.explanation: Blocking key base terms is more efficient and secure, because the algorithm then blocks weak variants and combinations.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Eliminate bad passwords using Microsoft Entra Password Protection”, “Custom banned password list” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: Instead, it's much more efficient and secure to block only the key base terms, such as the following examples: - "Contoso" - "London" - "Widget" The password validation algorithm then automatically blocks weak variants and combinations.

notes.front: “Beacon” is banned. A user chooses “B3acon7x”. After normalisation and matching, it contains one banned term plus the characters 7 and x. Is it accepted?
notes.back: C: no; it scores 3 points, below the 5 needed.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, because it contains a number
B) Yes; it scores 8 points, one per character
C) No; it scores 3 points, below the 5 needed
D) No, because any banned term means rejection
notes.choicesExplained: A: containing a number does not decide acceptance. B counts the banned term’s letters separately; the whole term scores only one point. D: a strong enough password can be accepted despite a banned term.
notes.explanation: Each banned term found scores one point and each remaining character one point; five points are needed.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Eliminate bad passwords using Microsoft Entra Password Protection”, “Score Calculation” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: Each banned password found in a user's password is given one point. 1. Each remaining character that isn't part of a banned password is given one point. 1. A password must be at least five (5) points to be accepted.

notes.front: Sign-in logs show one address trying “Spring2026!” once against each of 4,000 accounts, then moving on to the next common password. What attack is this?
notes.back: D: a password spray attack.
notes.choices:
A) A targeted guessing attack on one account
B) An MFA fatigue attack
C) A device code phishing attack
D) A password spray attack
notes.choicesExplained: A would try many passwords on a single account, the opposite pattern. B floods one user with approval prompts. C tricks a user into entering a code on another device.
notes.explanation: Spray attacks submit a few of the weakest known passwords against each account to avoid detection thresholds.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Eliminate bad passwords using Microsoft Entra Password Protection”, “Password spray attacks and third-party compromised password lists” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: Instead, most password spray attacks submit only a few of the known weakest passwords against each of the accounts in an enterprise.

notes.front: A ministry signs staff in with smart-card certificates through on-premises federation servers, and wants to retire those servers. Which Microsoft Entra method lets users authenticate with their X.509 certificates directly?
notes.back: A: certificate-based authentication.
notes.choices:
A) Certificate-based authentication
B) A Temporary Access Pass
C) Voice call verification
D) Password writeback
notes.choicesExplained: B is a temporary passcode. C is a secondary phone method and uses no certificate. D copies password changes on-premises.
notes.explanation: It checks certificates directly against the Microsoft Entra identity, removing the need for federated infrastructure.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Certificate-based authentication”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A board asks which two measures, together, Microsoft says stop more than 99.9% of common identity-related attacks. What is the answer?
notes.back: A: using multifactor authentication and blocking legacy authentication.
notes.choices:
A) Using multifactor authentication and blocking legacy authentication
B) A custom banned password list and self-service password reset
C) Longer passwords and more frequent password changes
D) Password writeback and Temporary Access Passes
notes.choicesExplained: C, B and D are useful controls, but Microsoft’s 99.9% figure refers only to multifactor authentication combined with blocking legacy authentication.
notes.explanation: Microsoft bases this figure on its own learnings, and builds both measures into security defaults.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: Based on our learnings more than 99.9% of those common identity-related attacks are stopped by using multifactor authentication and blocking legacy authentication.

notes.front: An admin turns on security defaults. Which of these does it not do?
notes.back: B: apply a custom banned password list.
notes.choices:
A) Require all users to register for multifactor authentication
B) Apply a custom banned password list
C) Block legacy authentication protocols
D) Require multifactor authentication to use the Azure portal
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D are all among the basic controls security defaults include. Custom banned terms belong to Microsoft Entra Password Protection.
notes.explanation: Security defaults cover MFA registration and prompts, blocking legacy authentication and device code flow, and protecting privileged activities.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: These basic controls include: - Requiring all users to register for multifactor authentication - Requiring administrators to do multifactor authentication - Requiring users to do multifactor authentication when necessary - Blocking legacy authentication protocols - Blocking device code flow - Protecting privileged activities like access to the Azure portal

notes.front: A licensed user whom the admin has enabled for SSPR tries to reset her password, but the process stops. She never set up any verification method. What is missing?
notes.back: B: registration of the authentication methods she wants to use.
notes.choices:
A) Password writeback
B) Registration of the authentication methods she wants to use
C) A premium Conditional Access policy
D) A Temporary Access Pass issued every time
notes.choicesExplained: A matters only when the password is managed on-premises. C is not one of the course’s SSPR requirements. D is for onboarding or recovery sign-in, not an SSPR prerequisite.
notes.explanation: SSPR needs a licence, enablement by an administrator and registered methods; she has only the first two.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe self-service password reset”, “How self-service password reset works”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: During a test, an admin wants to switch off Microsoft’s global banned password list for one tenant and rely only on the custom list. What happens?
notes.back: B: it can’t be done; the global list always applies and is combined with any custom list.
notes.choices:
A) The admin disables it in the tenant settings
B) It can’t be done; the global list always applies and is combined with any custom list
C) It is off until a premium licence is bought
D) Adding custom terms replaces the global list
notes.choicesExplained: A is impossible because the list can’t be disabled. C is wrong because it applies automatically. D is wrong because custom terms are combined with the global list.
notes.explanation: The global list is applied automatically to all users, needs no configuration and can’t be disabled.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Eliminate bad passwords using Microsoft Entra Password Protection”, “Global banned password list” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: The global banned password list is automatically applied to all users in a Microsoft Entra tenant. There's nothing to enable or configure, and can't be disabled.

notes.front: A user signs in with a password and a code shown on a hardware key. Which two factor categories has she used?
notes.back: A: something you know and something you have.
notes.choices:
A) Something you know and something you have
B) Something you have and something you are
C) Something you know, twice
D) Something you are and something you know
notes.choicesExplained: C and D would need two knowledge factors or a biometric; B would need a biometric such as a fingerprint instead of the password.
notes.explanation: A password is something you know; a trusted device not easily duplicated, like a hardware key, is something you have.
notes.source: Microsoft, “How it works: Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication”, “How it works: Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: Something you know, typically a password. * Something you have, such as a trusted device that's not easily duplicated, like a phone or hardware key.

notes.front: Device-bound versus synced passkeys: where does the private key live?
notes.back: Device-bound: on one physical device, never leaving it. Synced: synced across the user’s devices through a cloud passkey provider.
notes.explanation: Examples differ accordingly: security keys and Authenticator versus iCloud Keychain or Google Password Manager.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Passkeys (FIDO2)”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Security defaults versus Conditional Access: which needs a Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 licence?
notes.back: Conditional Access. Security defaults come at no extra cost.
notes.explanation: Conditional Access gives more granular control for organisations with complex requirements.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe multifactor authentication”, “Conditional Access and multifactor authentication”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to Microsoft, are security defaults likely right for an organisation that already has premium Microsoft Entra ID licences?
notes.back: Probably not; such organisations, or those with complex requirements, should consider Conditional Access.
notes.explanation: Microsoft keeps the hedge: security defaults are “probably not right” for them, not forbidden.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Who should use Conditional Access?” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.sourceLicence: B · MIT
notes.evidence: If you're an organization with Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 licenses, security defaults are probably not right for you. - If your organization has complex security requirements, you should consider Conditional Access.

notes.front: Global versus custom banned password list: who supplies the terms?
notes.back: Global: Microsoft, from security telemetry. Custom: the organisation, with its own specific terms.
notes.explanation: The global list applies automatically; the custom list is added on top and combined with it.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe password protection and management capabilities”, “Global banned password list”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Microsoft Authenticator mode is primary-only, and which works as both primary and secondary for MFA and SSPR?
notes.back: Passwordless sign-in is primary only; push notification works as primary and for MFA and SSPR.
notes.explanation: The same app can play different roles depending on the mode used.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Describe authentication methods”, “Primary and secondary authentication”
